source_title: Obstetric triage improvement process using the Donabedian model of quality care: a quality improvement initiative
locator: Methods, baseline audit and sample; Results, Figure 1 (arrival-after-registration to initial nursing assessment).
source_setting: Labor-and-delivery triage at a tertiary hospital in Pakistan; booked patients >=24 weeks gestation were assessed there, while unbooked or <24-week patients went to the emergency department.
source_period: Baseline audit during the first quarter of 2018; post-intervention audit after six PDSA cycles; exact post-audit dates and intervention duration are not consistently reported.
source_n: Convenience audit sample n=200 (100 pre, 100 post); facility handled about 400-500 triage visits/month, which is throughput context rather than the audit denominator.
quantity: Share meeting a 5-minute arrival-to-initial-nursing-assessment target, pre vs post redesign
source_evidence_basis: The paper's pre/post audit reports 6% meeting the 5-minute target before redesign and 65% afterward. The redesign included acuity-based prioritization, assigned triage roles, a two-stage assessment and handoff, staffing/training changes, and recurring audits.
limitations: Single-site quality-improvement project in a tertiary Pakistan hospital; small convenience samples and bundled PDSA changes limit causal attribution. The intervention is described as a six-month project, but exact post-audit dates are not provided. Not an RWJ measurement or a clinical triage rule.
inferred_scenario_use: Model arrival, brief initial screen, acuity-based queue priority, assessment-room handoff, and onward disposition as distinct states; retain the reported before/after proportions only as external process context, never as RWJ performance targets.

source_title: Obstetric triage improvement process using the Donabedian model of quality care: a quality improvement initiative
locator: Results, Figure 2 and text on length of stay; endpoint is time in L&D triage, not delivery admission-to-discharge duration.
source_setting: Same tertiary-hospital L&D triage service in Pakistan.
source_period: Baseline audit during first quarter 2018; post-intervention audit after six PDSA cycles; exact post-audit dates are not reported.
source_n: Convenience audit sample n=200 (100 pre, 100 post). Pre-intervention LOS was undocumented for 16% in the initial baseline review; charted LOS ranges are reported for the audited cohort.
quantity: Reported L&D-triage length of stay range and post-audit patient shares
unit: minutes; post shares are percent of audited patients
source_evidence_basis: The paper reports pre-intervention triage LOS from 30 to 240 minutes, with 64% meeting a 120-minute local benchmark; after redesign it reports 75% with 30-minute LOS and 25% with 60-minute LOS.
limitations: The endpoint is triage visit duration, not labor, delivery, postpartum stay, or NICU length of stay. Small single-center convenience sample; baseline LOS was missing for some records and intervention package is bundled. The paper's narrative also summarizes LOS as 240 to 60 minutes, so retain the detailed reported range and shares rather than infer a common mean or distribution.
inferred_scenario_use: Keep triage LOS distinct from the subsequent labor-and-delivery and postpartum unit stays; use as a workflow segmentation clue and external observed range only, not a fitted service-time distribution.

source_title: Obstetric triage improvement process using the Donabedian model of quality care: a quality improvement initiative
locator: Methods, Problem and PDSA cycles; Results, post-implementation acuity distribution; process diagram and sixth PDSA cycle.
source_setting: Same tertiary Pakistan hospital; 24/7 triage for pregnancy concerns, labor and birth, medical complaints, and maternal-fetal surveillance.
source_period: Project initiated after a 2018 sentinel event; baseline audit first quarter 2018; six PDSA cycles; post-audit calendar window not specified.
source_n: Service context: >6,000 deliveries/year and 400-500 L&D triage visits/month. Post-implementation acuity distribution denominator is the 100-patient post-audit sample.
quantity: Documented post-redesign triage acuity categories and specified process sequence

workflow: direct labor-room or operating-theatre transfer for level-1 cases

unit: percent of post-audit patients; qualitative workflow sequence
source_evidence_basis: After implementation, the audit categorized 3% red, 5% amber, 77% green, and 15% white/non-urgent. The paper specifies an assigned triage nurse, brief first assessment, documentation, handoff to a second nurse, further assessment, and direct transfer to labor room or operating theatre for the highest urgency category.
limitations: This is a report of one hospital's locally adapted process and audit mix; category shares are not general prevalence estimates. Acuity labels and routing thresholds are institutional clinical content and must not be copied as treatment rules. Exact post-audit dates are absent.
inferred_scenario_use: Use only as a candidate maternity pathway structure: triage can discharge, continue evaluation, admit to labor-and-delivery, or route to a procedural area; model separate staff roles and handoff events. Require local clinical governance for all decision rules.

source_title: Mass intrahospital transport of the neonatal intensive care unit: a systems-based approach to safety, efficiency, and family-centered care
locator: Methods, Context assessment; Results, clinical and transport variables; Discussion, full transport cycle estimates by acuity.
source_setting: Two planned relocations of a 24-bed intensive/high-dependency area within a 42-bed quaternary NICU at Sidra Medicine, Doha; route 120-140 m.
source_period: Two relocations approximately one year apart; exact event dates not stated in the article. Published 27 May 2026.
source_n: 34 neonates transported (17 per relocation); 33 had complete analyzed documentation (16 in relocation 1, 17 in relocation 2). Acuity subgroup denominators for the estimated cycle bands are not provided.
quantity: Estimated full transport cycle from preparation through team return by acuity grouping
unit: minutes per neonate transport cycle (approximate planning estimates)
source_evidence_basis: Multidisciplinary simulation and observations informed approximate full-cycle times: 30-40 minutes for ventilated neonates on multiple inotropes and inhaled nitric oxide, 20-30 minutes for stable ventilated neonates, and 15-20 minutes for stable non-invasive or room-air neonates. Actual individual departure-to-arrival medians were 4 and 6 minutes in the two relocations, a different endpoint.
limitations: Single-center renovation relocation; cycle bands are planning estimates without subgroup sample counts and are not distributions. Actual individual movement time excludes much of preparation and return work. Not a routine inter-hospital transport time or RWJ value.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent destination readiness, pre-transport preparation, team allocation, movement, receiving handoff, post-arrival care, and team return as separate linked tasks; vary resource needs by locally approved acuity classes without encoding clinical thresholds.

source_title: Mass intrahospital transport of the neonatal intensive care unit: a systems-based approach to safety, efficiency, and family-centered care
locator: Methods, stakeholder/work-system design; Results, transport outcomes and staff survey; Table 2.
source_setting: Same quaternary NICU relocations; care area had 24 intensive/high-dependency beds within a 42-bed NICU.
source_period: Two planned relocations approximately one year apart; exact dates not stated.
source_n: 34 transported neonates (33 with complete case data); 57 staff survey responses after relocation 1 and 61 after relocation 2; survey response denominator not established.
quantity: Observed relocation duration and staff-reported operational support needs
unit: minutes per relocation; staff survey response percentages and qualitative comments
source_evidence_basis: Two transport teams worked in parallel; the planned 255-minute total was based on 30 minutes per infant, while actual 17-infant relocations took 225 and 197 minutes. Staff feedback after the first relocation requested more nursing support, and this request persisted after the second; IT/facilities/biomedical engineering standby support addressed infrastructure problems.
limitations: Small, highly organized planned relocation in a quaternary NICU; voluntary survey responses and no control group. Staff positive-response percentages are not staffing adequacy measures. This is not a regular-shift nurse-to-patient ratio or RWJ staffing evidence.
inferred_scenario_use: Model dedicated transport teams, bedside nurse accompaniment, parallel preparation, standby technical roles, equipment readiness, huddles, and extra-support contingencies as optional resources; do not infer staffing ratios from the survey.

source_title: Mass intrahospital transport of the neonatal intensive care unit: a systems-based approach to safety, efficiency, and family-centered care
locator: Methods, parent survey; Results, Parent survey and relocation communication plan.
source_setting: Same NICU relocation project; parent communication, satisfaction, perceived safety, continuity, and ability to accompany infant were surveyed.
source_period: After each of two relocations approximately one year apart; exact dates not stated.
source_n: 12 parents (70% of eligible parents) responded after each relocation.
quantity: Parent responses on information, satisfaction, and transfer participation
unit: respondents per relocation; qualitative reported concern
source_evidence_basis: All 12 responding parents after each move reported feeling informed and satisfied with transfer and post-transfer care. The article records one concern about not being able to accompany the infant during relocation 1 and describes advance letters, face-to-face updates, invitations to accompany, and post-transfer communication.
limitations: Small voluntary survey with about 70% response; parent experience may not represent nonresponders. Parent accompaniment depends on route and local safety/environment constraints. Not a family-role policy for RWJ.
inferred_scenario_use: Include family notification, optional accompaniment, and alternate update channels as workflow needs that can compete with transport timing and route constraints; validate local policy and family preferences.

source_title: Shift-to-shift handoffs in the NICU: lessons learned from a large scale audit
locator: Abstract, Study design and Results; family presence and participation among observed shift-to-shift handoffs.
source_setting: NICU provider and nursing shift handoffs at 40 centers in a learning collaborative.
source_period: 10-month audit period; exact calendar dates not stated. Published online 14 July 2023.
quantity: Family presence at handoff and active family participation conditional on presence
unit: percent; participation denominator is handoffs where family was present
source_evidence_basis: The multi-center observational audit reports family presence at 5.9% of handoffs; among handoffs where a family member was present, 48.2% included contribution of information, questions, or shared goals.
limitations: Audit measure from participating learning-collaborative centers, not a representative census of NICUs. Full article is subscription content; only primary publisher abstract was accessible in this review. These are handoff behavior observations, not family preference or quality-outcome estimates.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent shift handoff as a distinct transition and allow family presence/participation as an optional actor with locally defined access, consent, and timing; do not make the observed percentages target rates.

source_title: Inter-organizational pooling of NICU nurses in the Dutch neonatal network: a simulation-optimization study
locator: Section 2, operational-bed analysis; Section 3, model assumptions; Table 6 operational capacity occurrence.
source_setting: Nine-location Dutch national NICU network; operational-bed counts were self-reported through BabyZoektBed and depend on available nurses, physical beds, and patient acuity.
source_period: Operational-capacity empirical input: 2020; demand estimates: 2015-2019; simulation outcomes generated in 10-year steady-state runs with 10 replications and a 1-year warm-up.
source_n: Nine NICUs; 2020 operational-capacity input distribution summarized across network locations. Site-specific availability was not published for privacy reasons.
quantity: Empirical occurrence of weekly staffed operational capacity as share of maximum capacity
unit: percent of weeks in the study input distribution
source_evidence_basis: The model used a one-year 2020 empirical distribution of self-reported operational capacity; for example, 80% of maximum capacity occurred in half of observations. Authors also report individual NICUs had no operational bed available on average 53% of the time, with up to 82% at the most occupied site, but do not disclose the sites.
limitations: Dutch network and 2020 capacity conditions; self-reported source data, rounded input frequencies, site identities suppressed. The 1:2 nurse-to-bed ratio elsewhere in the model is an explicit simplifying assumption and should not be interpreted as a staffing standard. Neither capacity values nor results are RWJ observations.
inferred_scenario_use: Distinguish licensed/physical beds from operational staffed capacity and make capacity acuity-sensitive; only use this as an external model-design prompt, not as a numeric local calibration.

source_title: Inter-organizational pooling of NICU nurses in the Dutch neonatal network: a simulation-optimization study
locator: Section 4.3, baseline and flex-pool experiment results; Figures 6-10.
source_setting: Discrete-event simulation and integer-linear-program optimization of staffing and patient allocation across nine Dutch NICU locations; scenario pool shares nurses across organizations.
source_period: Empirical capacity input year 2020, patient-demand inputs 2015-2019; 10-year steady-state simulations with 10 replications after a one-year warm-up.
source_n: Nine NICU locations; simulated network-wide annual transport counts estimated from model output, not a patient-level study cohort.
quantity: Modeled annual patient transports under baseline vs five-flex-nurses-per-location, all-location sharing scenario
unit: percent of simulated patients and approximate transports/year
source_evidence_basis: In the model, five flex nurses per location with all nine locations participating reduced predicted patient transports by about 70%; the authors report mean 6.31% (95% CI 5.63%-6.98%) versus baseline 21.53% (95% CI 20.46%-22.60%). This is a modeled scenario, not observed intervention effect.
limitations: Results depend on Dutch geography, staffing-sharing feasibility, assumed shift timing, acuity and LOS inputs, and objective weights; model assumes patients/staff shift only at shift boundaries although real neonatal transfers occur through the day. The authors note real-world short-term capacity mitigations (such as moving infants to lower-care units) are not fully modeled. Not a local forecast or RWJ result.
inferred_scenario_use: Use the model structure to test whether operational nurse capacity, acuity, referral acceptance, network transfers, and step-down/discharge transitions should interact; do not import its effect size or assumptions as a local prediction.
